pedagogy.summary: By upper KS2, children connect everyday CHOICES to how the body's systems function — a step up from naming needs to reasoning about consequences. The core moves: exercise strengthens the heart, lungs and muscles; a poor diet high in sugar and fat leads to problems like tooth decay, unhealthy weight and heart disease; adequate sleep supports growth and function; and harmful substances (tobacco, alcohol, drugs) damage specific organs (smoking harms the lungs and raises heart-disease risk; alcohol harms the liver and affects the brain). The key conceptual leap is that effects are often CUMULATIVE and DELAYED — one biscuit or one late night is fine; it's the pattern over time that shapes health — which is exactly what makes healthy choices feel abstract to children. Teach it as mechanism, not moralising: link each choice to the body system it affects (drawing on the circulatory/respiratory/digestive systems already learned), and treat health messages as evidence-based claims to reason about rather than rules to obey. Handle sensitive content (weight, substances) factually and without stigma.
bestPractices: Explain choices through MECHANISM on already-learned systems ('smoking damages the alveoli so less oxygen reaches the blood'), so health advice is understood, not just memorised as rules.
Make the cumulative/delayed nature explicit — one choice vs a pattern over months/years — since children under-weight long-term effects; use timelines or repeated-choice models.

Ground claims in evidence and let children evaluate them (obtain-and-combine information, weigh a claim), matching the KS2 'recognise the impact of diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle' objective and its argument-from-evidence character.
Connect to the child's own measurable body (resting vs post-exercise heart rate from the earlier topic) to make 'exercise strengthens the heart' concrete and personal.
Teach sensitive topics (weight, tobacco, alcohol) factually, focusing on body systems and risk (not certainty) and avoiding shame or moralising language.
keyRepresentations: Choice→system→effect chains (e.g. exercise → heart/lungs → stronger; smoking → lungs → less oxygen, higher heart-disease risk)
A timeline / repeated-choice model showing cumulative effects building over time
Body-systems dashboard linking each choice to the organ system it affects
Risk framing (increases the CHANCE of disease) rather than deterministic outcomes
Personal evidence: own resting vs post-exercise pulse as proof exercise trains the heart
commonMisconceptions: 'One unhealthy thing will make you ill / one healthy thing keeps you well' — missing that it's the cumulative pattern that matters.
'You can see straight away if something is unhealthy' — missing the delayed onset of many effects.
'Being thin = healthy and being larger = unhealthy' — conflating body size with health; focus on systems and behaviours, factually and without stigma.
'Some foods are poison / totally banned' — rather than amount-and-frequency within an overall balance.
'Exercise is only about losing weight' — missing that it strengthens the heart, lungs and muscles regardless of weight.
'Smoking/alcohol only harm you when you're old' — missing that damage accumulates from the start.
'Health outcomes are certain' — rather than changes in RISK/probability.

learn.summary: For upper KS2 (ages 9–11), move children from naming healthy behaviours to reasoning about how everyday choices affect specific body systems, and crucially that effects are usually cumulative and delayed — it is the pattern over months and years, not a single biscuit or late night, that shapes health. Teach through MECHANISM on systems already studied (circulatory, respiratory, digestive), frame outcomes as changes in RISK not certainty, and handle sensitive content (weight, substances) factually and without stigma. Core activity: a 'lifestyle over time' simulation where repeated choices compound, complemented by an evidence-weighing conversation with an expert, a tap-to-reveal body reference, a personal-pulse measurement, and consolidation items matching choice to internal effect.

activities.title: Lifestyle over time: watch choices compound
feedback: When a learner expects one bad choice to tank a gauge, point out the slow drift and invite them to run several weeks of the same choice to see the pattern emerge.
If a learner reads the risk meter as a guaranteed outcome, clarify it shows an increased CHANCE of disease, not a certainty.
Keep the weight gauge framed as one body-system indicator among several, not as the overall measure of health, so body size is not conflated with health.
When tapping a gauge, tie the effect back to the system the child already studied so the advice is understood as mechanism, not an arbitrary rule.
activities.rationale: The hard, distinctive idea is delayed, cumulative causality. A simulation where weekly choices are set and body-system indicators drift across a compressed timeline makes that accumulation visible and manipulable, and lets hover/tap explanations surface mechanism and risk. Side-by-side replay makes 'pattern over time' concrete rather than moralised. Gauge drift rates and magnitudes are qualitative design illustrations, not sourced health figures.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils should recognise the impact of diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle on the way their bodies function.

A balanced diet, regular physical activity, adequate sleep and avoiding tobacco/harmful alcohol use support health; poor diet and smoking increase risk of conditions including heart disease, and effects accumulate over time.
learnerActions: Steer a character week by week, setting choices each simulated week: meals, how much exercise, how much sleep, and whether to smoke or drink.
Watch heart, lung, weight and energy gauges respond slowly — notice that no single choice moves the needle much.

Run the clock forward across many weeks and observe patterns compounding: a mostly-active, balanced character's heart and lung gauges strengthen, while a sedentary, high-sugar, smoking character's gauges drift the other way and the disease-risk meter rises — toward a higher CHANCE, not a certainty.
Replay two lifestyles side by side to compare how accumulation over time, not any one day, built the difference.
Tap any gauge to read how that choice acts on the actual body system (e.g. 'smoking damages the alveoli so less oxygen reaches the blood').
activities.intendedInsight: Health is built or eroded by the accumulation of everyday choices over time; single choices barely register, but repeated patterns change how body systems function and shift the RISK of disease.

activities.title: Ask the doctor: weigh a health claim
feedback: When a learner asserts a claim, prompt them to give the evidence or mechanism behind it rather than accepting it as a rule.
For sensitive topics (weight, tobacco, alcohol), keep responses factual, focused on body systems and risk, and free of shame or moralising.
activities.rationale: The topic has a genuine obtain-and-evaluate-information dimension that an in-role expert conversation may serve well, and that suits sensitive content handled factually. It is intended to complement the simulation; a dialogue is less able to make the cumulative dynamic felt. Efficacy of this interaction is untested.
learnerActions: Ask a friendly doctor or body-systems scientist your real questions in role, e.g. 'what does smoking actually do to my lungs?'
Weigh the answer, which is grounded in mechanism and risk, and respond when gently probed ('why do you think that?').
Bring an evidence question to settle, e.g. 'what's my evidence that exercise makes the heart stronger, not just the arm and leg muscles?'
activities.intendedInsight: Health messages are evidence-based claims to reason about, not rules to obey; you can obtain information from an expert and combine it with what you know to judge a claim.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal body: choice to organ
feedback: If a learner says smoking only harms the lungs, point them to the heart-disease-risk link too, and note harm accumulates from the start.

If a learner treats exercise as only about losing weight, highlight that regular exercise strengthens the heart muscle and the breathing muscles, and helps the body use oxygen better, whatever a person's weight.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal body is a useful mechanism reference. It is a static reference layer and does not itself convey the accumulation-over-time that defines the concept, so it supports rather than replaces the timeline work.
sourceClaims: A balanced diet, regular physical activity, adequate sleep and avoiding tobacco/harmful alcohol use support health; poor diet and smoking increase risk of conditions including heart disease, and effects accumulate over time.
learnerActions: Tap an organ on a body diagram to reveal how diet, exercise, smoking and alcohol affect it.

Build a choice-to-system-to-effect chain for each organ, e.g. exercise to heart and breathing muscles to stronger; smoking to lungs to less oxygen and higher heart-disease risk; sugary diet to teeth (higher risk of decay) and a diet high in saturated fat to heart and blood vessels (higher heart-disease risk); alcohol to liver and brain.
Use it as a reference layer to check mechanism links encountered in the simulation.
activities.intendedInsight: Each lifestyle choice acts on a specific body system, so health advice can be understood mechanistically rather than memorised as isolated rules.

activities.title: Connect it to your own pulse
feedback: If a learner thinks exercise only affects limb muscles, connect the raised pulse to the heart working harder as a muscle of its own.

Distinguish the two measurements: the immediate post-exercise rise shows effort now, while a resting pulse that is consistently lower after a sustained period of regular activity, measured under similar conditions, would be evidence that fits with the heart strengthening — reinforcing the cumulative idea in their own body, though some children may see little change in a few weeks.
activities.rationale: Connecting to the child's own measurable body is intended to make an abstract claim concrete and personal, and to reinforce the evidence-based stance. The specific heart-strengthening-via-pulse mechanism is a pedagogy inference rather than a directly cited source claim, and the activity is a proposal; the immediate pulse rise and long-term resting-pulse change are kept distinct so neither is overclaimed.
learnerActions: Measure your resting heart rate, then your heart rate just after exercise, drawing on the earlier heart-rate topic.

Use the immediate difference as evidence that the heart works harder during exercise; and, over a period of regular activity, compare your resting pulse before and after that period to look for adaptation, taking several readings at the same time of day and when calm, and remembering that resting pulse also changes with things like illness, tiredness or excitement, so a small change may not show adaptation.
Explain what this shows about exercise working the heart itself, not just the arm and leg muscles.
activities.intendedInsight: Exercise works the heart itself: a pulse that rises during and after exercise shows the heart working harder, and a resting pulse that stays lower (measured carefully under similar conditions) after a sustained period of regular activity fits with the heart adapting and strengthening over time — not just a slogan, and not only about limb muscles.

activities.title: Consolidate: match, judge, interpret
feedback: If a learner judges health only by looking slim or feeling fine, ask what the heart, arteries, lungs or teeth are doing out of sight.

If a learner says exercise cancels smoking, separate the two: exercise strengthens the heart and breathing muscles while smoking still damages the lungs and raises heart-disease risk — one does not erase the other.
If a learner bans whole foods as 'poison', reframe around amount and frequency within an overall balance.
activities.rationale: A matching/claim-judging/data-interpretation set consolidates the choice-to-effect core and surfaces common misconceptions for reteaching. Recognition and short items assess and reinforce but do not by themselves elicit the extended reasoning the simulation and conversation target.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils should recognise the impact of diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle on the way their bodies function.
learnerActions: Match each choice to the body-system effect it causes.
Judge a given health claim as reasonable or not and say why, using mechanism and risk.
Interpret a simple data/timeline item showing how an effect builds up cumulatively over time.

Reason about transfer cases: how two people of the same weight can differ in heart health; why a frequently sugary diet raises the risk of tooth decay even without weight gain; whether a fit marathon runner's exercise cancels out their smoking.
activities.intendedInsight: You can distinguish health from mere appearance by naming a specific internal harm, and you can read cumulative effects from data over time.

constraints: Teach sensitive topics (weight, tobacco, alcohol) factually, focusing on body systems and risk, and avoiding shame or moralising language; do not conflate body size with health.
Frame outcomes as changes in RISK/probability, not deterministic certainties ('increases the chance of heart disease', not 'will give you heart disease').
Make the cumulative/delayed nature explicit: contrast one choice with a pattern over months and years, since children under-weight long-term effects.
Explain choices through mechanism on already-learned systems (circulatory, respiratory, digestive) rather than presenting health rules to obey.

When using pulse evidence, keep the immediate post-exercise rise (heart working harder now) distinct from a lowered resting pulse after sustained activity (evidence of adaptation); do not treat one elevated reading as proof the heart has strengthened.
The tap-to-reveal body diagram is a static reference layer: it supports mechanism links but does not convey accumulation over time, so pair it with the timeline/simulation work.

Matching and multiple-choice items assess and reinforce recognition; they do not by themselves elicit the independent reasoning about cumulative, delayed effects that the simulation and expert conversation target.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a 3D artefact as 'adding nothing' and asserted a static image 'cannot' convey accumulation and a quiz 'can't build' the central idea; these are internal ranking comparative/necessity claims not established by the cited sources. They have been softened to scoped affordances/limits (a static diagram is a reference layer; recognition items reinforce but do not elicit extended construction).

The expert-conversation and personal-pulse activities carry empty sourceClaims because neither cited source directly supports those specific interactions or the heart-strengthening-via-pulse mechanism; they are conservative, qualified proposals.

The pulse activity's insight was tightened: an immediate elevated pulse evidences the heart working harder, whereas a lowered resting pulse over a period of regular activity is the evidence of strengthening/adaptation; the two were previously conflated.
The curriculum source (DfE) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim as an objective reference rather than independently confirmed here.

The simulation's specific gauge behaviours (exact rates of drift, which choices move which gauges) are design illustrations, not quantified from the sources; keep them qualitative and avoid presenting invented numeric health outcomes.

probeDeeper: How can two people weigh exactly the same but one has a much healthier heart? What could make the difference?
Why does a poor, sugary diet cause tooth decay even in someone who never gains weight?
A marathon runner smokes. They're very fit. Does the exercise cancel out the smoking? Why or why not?
What's your evidence that exercise makes the heart stronger, not just the arm and leg muscles?
assess.correctAnswer: These choices damage the body internally even without a visible weight change: sugary food causes tooth decay and, with fatty food, raises the risk of heart disease; lack of exercise leaves the heart, lungs and muscles weaker; smoking damages the lungs and increases heart-disease risk. Looking slim or feeling fine doesn't mean the heart, arteries, lungs or teeth aren't being harmed.

errorPatterns.pattern: health is about weight and looks — 'if you're slim and feel fine, you're healthy'
errorPatterns.nextMove: separate outward appearance from internal system health; ask what the heart, arteries and teeth are doing out of sight
errorPatterns.distractor: If you're slim and feel fine, your body is healthy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: judges health only by appearance and denies any hidden internal harm

errorPatterns.pattern: smoking only harms the lungs, nothing else (or 'a bit of smoking won't hurt')
errorPatterns.nextMove: link smoking to both lung damage and heart-disease risk, and note harm accumulates over time
errorPatterns.distractor: Smoking only harms your lungs, nothing else.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names only the lungs and misses the raised heart-disease risk, or dismisses small amounts as harmless

errorPatterns.pattern: foods are simply good or bad — some foods are 'poison' to be banned entirely
errorPatterns.nextMove: reframe around balance and quantity — most foods are fine in the right amount — not forbidden foods
errorPatterns.revealedBy: forbids whole foods rather than talking about amounts and balance

errorPatterns.pattern: exercise is only for losing weight
errorPatterns.nextMove: connect exercise to a stronger heart muscle and greater lung capacity, not just weight
errorPatterns.revealedBy: cannot say exercise strengthens the heart, lungs and muscles, only that it burns fat

responseLevels.gap: Equates health with appearance or feeling fine; cannot name any way an unhealthy choice harms the body internally.
responseLevels.full: Links specific choices to specific internal effects (exercise→heart/lung/muscle strength; sugar→tooth decay; fatty diet and smoking→heart-disease risk) and explains that internal harm can occur despite a normal outward appearance; transfers to a new case such as the fit smoker or two same-weight people with different heart health.
responseLevels.partial: Lists healthy and unhealthy choices and some effects (obesity, tooth decay, weakness) as separate facts, but cannot connect a specific choice to a specific internal system, or still thinks looking slim means being healthy.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Someone says: 'I'm slim and I feel fine, so it doesn't matter that I eat lots of sugary, fatty food, never exercise, and I've started smoking.' Choose one part of the body that is being harmed anyway, even though they look fine — and explain what is actually happening inside that they can't see.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who equates health with looking slim and feeling fine cannot name a hidden internal harm. A child with the real idea names an internal system — heart, arteries, lungs or teeth — being damaged despite a normal outward appearance.
